What is Go: Go is a compiled, statically-typed language designed for simplicity, concurrency, and fast execution. Built by Google for systems programming and microservices. Common mistake: assuming Go is like Java/C# — Go has no classes, no inheritance, no exceptions, and no generics (pre-1.18). Best practice: embrace Go's simplicity — prefer composition over inheritance, use explicit error returns instead of exceptions, and leverage goroutines for concurrency.
Go Syntax: Go syntax emphasizes clarity and brevity. Uses curly braces for blocks and semicolons are optional. Comments use // or /* */. Common mistake: placing the opening brace on a new line — Go requires the opening brace on the same line as the declaration (enforced by gofmt). Best practice: run gofmt or go fmt on all code to enforce canonical formatting; use meaningful names even for short variables.
Your First Program: Every Go program starts with a package declaration and a main() function for executables. The package must be 'main' for a runnable binary. Common mistake: using 'print' or 'println' for serious output — prefer fmt.Println for formatted output to stdout. Best practice: structure all real programs with package main, a main() function, and use imports for standard library packages rather than built-in print.
Go Playground: The Go Playground (go.dev/play) lets you write, run, and share Go code in your browser. Great for experimentation and sharing bug repros.
go run vs go build: go run compiles and runs a program without producing a binary. go build produces a standalone executable in the current directory.

# Run directly (no binary)
go run main.go

# Build an executable
# Produces ./program (or .exe on Windows)
go build -o program main.go
GOPATH & Module Basics: GOPATH was the original workspace location. Modern Go uses modules (go mod) instead. GOPATH is still used for global binary installs via go install.

export GOPATH=$HOME/go
# Install a tool globally
go install golang.org/x/tools/cmd/goimports@latest
# Installed binaries go to $GOPATH/bin

Variable Declaration: Declare variables using var, const, or short declaration (:=). Types can be explicit or inferred. Common mistake: using := outside a function — it only works inside function bodies; package-level declarations require var or const. Best practice: use := for local variables with clear initialization; use var for zero-value declarations (var x int); use const for compile-time constants. Scope and shadowing: inner scopes can redeclare a name from an outer scope — the inner declaration shadows the outer one. Always check that you haven't accidentally shadowed a package-level variable inside a function using :=.
Primitive Types: Go includes bool, string, int, uint, float32, float64, complex64, and more. Integer types have fixed sizes (int8, int16, int32, int64). Rune is an alias for int32 representing a Unicode code point. Complex numbers (complex64, complex128) are first-class with real+imag syntax. String literals come in two forms: raw (backtick-quoted, no escapes) and interpreted (double-quoted, supports \n, \t, etc.). Common mistake: confusing int and int64 — int is platform-dependent (32 or 64 bit); int64 is always 64 bit. Use int unless you need a specific size.

var active bool = true
var score int64 = 1000
var ratio float32 = 2.5
var c complex128 = 1 + 2i

// Rune — Unicode code point
type rune = int32
var r rune = '\u0041' // 'A'
var han rune = '世'    // Chinese character

// Raw vs interpreted strings
raw := `hello\nworld`   // literal backslash-n
interp := "hello\nworld" // actual newline
Type Conversion: Explicitly convert between compatible types using T(value) syntax. Go does NOT do implicit type conversion.
Constants: Constants are immutable values that must be known at compile time. Use const keyword with iota for enumerated constants. iota resets to 0 in each const block and increments by 1 for each line. Common mistake: thinking constants can be computed at runtime — they must be determinable at compile time, so function calls or runtime expressions don't work. Best practice: use iota for sequential numeric enums; use typed constants (const X type = val) for type safety; use untyped constants for flexibility in expressions.
Zero Values: Variables declared without an explicit initial value are assigned a zero value: 0 for numbers, false for bool, "" for strings, nil for pointers/slices/maps/channels/interfaces.

var i int     // 0
var f float64 // 0
var b bool    // false
var s string  // ""
var p *int    // nil
fmt.Println(i, f, b, s, p)
Short Declaration (:=): Use := inside functions for type-inferred variable declaration and assignment. Cannot use at package level. At least one variable on left must be new.

name := "Alice"
age := 30
// Re-declaration with new variable
age, year := 31, 2026 // age reassigned, year new
Type Inference: Go infers types from the right-hand side of := or var declarations. Untyped numeric constants get default types (int, float64, complex128) when needed.

x := 42       // int
pi := 3.14    // float64
c := 1 + 2i   // complex128

var y float64 = 3
z := y         // z is float64 (inferred from y)

Arithmetic Operators: Standard math: +, -, *, /, %. Go supports ++ and -- but only as statements, not expressions.

x := 10 + 5
y := 20 - 3
z := 4 * 5
q := 20 / 4
r := 17 % 5
x++ // statement, OK
// y = x++ // compile error
Comparison Operators: Compare values using ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=. Return boolean results. Valid for comparable types.
Logical Operators: Combine booleans with &&, ||, and !. Short-circuit evaluation is supported: && stops on first false, || stops on first true.
Bitwise Operators: Manipulate bits using &, |, ^, <<, >>, and &^ (AND NOT, a.k.a. bit clear).
Increment/Decrement Statements: ++ and -- are statements, not expressions. They cannot be used in assignments or comparisons. Only postfix notation is allowed.
Operator Precedence: Go operator precedence from highest to lowest: *, /, %, <<, >>, &, &^; then +, -, |, ^; then ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=; then &&; then ||. Use parentheses to clarify.

If & Else: Standard conditional branching. Parentheses are optional; braces are required. If can include a short statement before the condition.
Switch Statement: Multi-way branching on a single expression. Cases don't fall through by default. Use fallthrough keyword explicitly when needed.

switch day {
case "Monday":
	fmt.Println("Work day")
case "Saturday", "Sunday":
	fmt.Println("Weekend")
default:
	fmt.Println("Other day")
}
For Loop: Go has only one loop construct. Use for with init, condition, and post, or as while/infinite loop.
Break & Continue: Exit loops early with break or skip to next iteration with continue. Labels let you break/continue outer loops.
Label Statements: Labels mark a position in code for break, continue, or goto. Use them to exit or continue outer loops from nested inner loops.
Type Switch: A switch that asserts the dynamic type of an interface value. Each case specifies a type. Useful with interface{} or any.

var v any = 42
switch t := v.(type) {
case int:
	fmt.Printf("int: %d\n", t)
case string:
	fmt.Printf("string: %s\n", t)
default:
	fmt.Printf("unknown: %T\n", t)
}
Defer: Defer postpones a function call until the surrounding function returns. Deferred calls are executed in LIFO order. Arguments are evaluated immediately.
Goto: Goto jumps to a labeled statement within the same function. Cannot jump over variable declarations or into blocks. Use sparingly — goto is widely discouraged in idiomatic Go. Prefer structured control flow (for, if/else, switch) over goto. The only acceptable uses are breaking out of deeply nested loops or error cleanup in generated code.

i := 0
loop:
if i < 3 {
	fmt.Println(i)
	i++
	goto loop
}

Function Declaration: Define functions with func keyword. Specify parameter types and return types explicitly.
Multiple Return Values: Functions can return multiple values. Commonly used for (result, error) pattern.
Named Return Values: Name return values for cleaner code. They act as variables initialized to zero values. A bare return returns the current values of named returns.
Variadic Functions: Accept variable number of arguments using ... syntax. Creates a slice of the arguments. Only the last parameter can be variadic.
Anonymous Functions & Closures: Functions without a name assigned to variables or passed directly. Closures capture surrounding variables by reference, not by value.
init Functions: init() runs automatically when a package is initialized, before main(). Multiple init() calls in a file run in order; across files they run in lexical order. No parameters or return values.
Function Values: Functions are first-class values in Go. They can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions (higher-order functions).

Arrays: Fixed-size sequences with homogeneous elements. Size is part of the type ([3]int != [4]int). Passed by value (copied) when assigned or passed to functions.
Slices: Dynamic-length views backed by an underlying array. Slice expression [low:high] creates a view into an existing array or slice without copying data.

nums := []int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
part := nums[1:4]  // [2, 3, 4]
nums = append(nums, 6) // may allocate new backing array
fmt.Println(len(nums), cap(nums))
Slice Internals: A slice is a descriptor: pointer to underlying array, length, capacity. Append grows by doubling the capacity up to 1024, then ~25% growth. Slicing beyond len but within cap reuses the backing array.

s := make([]int, 3, 5) // len=3, cap=5
s2 := s[:5]            // extends view to cap
s[0] = 10
fmt.Println(s2[0])      // 10 (same backing array)

copy(s2, []int{1,2,3,4,5}) // copy elements
Maps: Unordered key-value collections built on hash tables. Keys must be comparable types (== works). Maps are reference types; zero value is nil.
Range Loops: Iterate with range over slices, maps, strings, channels. For slices: returns index, value. For maps: returns key, value. For strings: returns byte index, rune.
make vs new: make(T, args) creates slices, maps, and channels (initialized, ready to use). new(T) allocates zero value and returns *T. make returns T (not *T).

s := make([]int, 5)    // slice ready to use
m := make(map[int]string) // map ready for insertion

p := new(int)    // *int pointing to 0
*p = 42
fmt.Println(*p)

// new for struct
u := new(User)   // *User with zero fields

Pointer Basics: Pointers hold memory addresses. Use & to get a variable's address and * to dereference (read or write through the pointer). Zero value is nil. Go has automatic memory management with garbage collection — allocated memory is freed when no references remain. Unlike C/C++, you don't manually free memory. The GC runs concurrently with a short STW pause. Escape analysis determines whether values live on the stack or heap: if a pointer escapes the function scope, the value is heap-allocated.

x := 42
p := &x         // p points to x, type *int
fmt.Println(*p) // 42 (dereference)
*p = 100        // changes x to 100
fmt.Println(x)  // 100
Pointers to Structs: Access struct fields through pointers using dot notation. Go automatically dereferences struct pointers for field access.
Pointers as Parameters: Go is pass-by-value. Use pointers to allow a function to modify its caller's data, or to avoid copying large structs.
new() Function: new(T) allocates zero-value storage for T and returns *T. It never returns nil. Equivalent to &T{} for structs. Use when you need a pointer to a zero-valued instance.
Pointer vs Value Receiver: Use pointer receiver (*T) when the method modifies the receiver, or when the struct is large. Use value receiver (T) for small, immutable types. Pointer receiver avoids copying on each call.

Struct Definition: Group related fields into a struct type. Exported fields start with uppercase letter for visibility across packages.
Struct Tags: Struct tags are metadata strings attached to fields, commonly used by encoding/json, validation libraries, and ORMs. Tags appear after the field type in backticks.
Anonymous (Embedded) Fields: Embed types without a field name. Their methods and fields are promoted to the embedding struct. Not inheritance, but composition.
Struct Methods: Attach methods to types using receiver syntax. Methods are functions with a receiver parameter between func and method name.
Pointer Receivers: Pointer receiver allows modification of the struct. Value receiver works on a copy. Consistency: if any method has pointer receiver, all should.
Struct Comparison: Structs with only comparable fields (no slices, maps, or functions) can be compared with == and used as map keys.
Constructor Functions: Go has no constructors. Use factory functions (NewXxx or New) that return a pointer to a struct, optionally performing validation or initialization.

Interface Definition: Define interfaces as a set of method signatures. Any type implementing all methods implicitly satisfies the interface. Interfaces are satisfied implicitly. Methods vs functions: a method is a function with a receiver parameter (func (t Type) MethodName()). Methods can only be defined on types within the same package. Functions are standalone (func Name()). Use methods when behavior depends on receiver state; use functions for stateless operations. Prefer methods for types that model domain concepts.
Implicit Implementation: Go uses structural typing. A type satisfies an interface simply by implementing its methods. No explicit declaration like 'implements' is needed.
Type Assertions: Extract the concrete value from an interface using value.(Type). The two-value form prevents panics: val, ok := x.(Type).
Empty Interface (any): interface{} (or 'any' in Go 1.18+) accepts values of any type. Used before generics for containers. Now used when truly any type is needed.
Interface Composition: Combine interfaces by embedding them in a new interface. A type must implement all embedded interfaces' methods to satisfy the composed interface.
Interface Values & Nil: An interface value is a (type, value) pair. An interface is nil only when both the type and value are nil. A nil pointer inside a non-nil interface is not nil!
Best Practices (Accept interfaces, retur: Accept interfaces to allow flexibility from callers; return concrete types so callers can access fields and methods without type assertions.

Error Interface: Errors are values implementing the built-in error interface: Error() string. Functions return nil to indicate success.
Error Checking: Idiomatic Go checks errors immediately. Use guard clauses for early returns. Handle errors once — don't ignore or handle them multiple times. For debugging, use stack traces: when a panic occurs, Go prints the full goroutine stack. Use debug.PrintStack() or runtime/debug.Stack() to capture stacks without panicking. The errors package can also include stack information with libraries like pkg/errors or fmt.Errorf+%w for error chains.
Custom Error Types: Create custom error types by implementing the Error() string method. Custom types carry additional context for callers to inspect.
Sentinel Errors: Sentinel errors are predefined error variables (convention: names start with Err) used as sentinel values for specific failure conditions. Compare with == or use errors.Is.
Error Wrapping: Use fmt.Errorf with %w to wrap errors, preserving the original error for errors.Is and errors.As. %W (uppercase) is NOT valid; use lowercase %w.
errors.Is and errors.As: errors.Is(err, target) checks if any error in the chain matches target. errors.As(err, targetType) finds the first error of a given type. Both work through wrapping layers.
Panic & Recover: Panic stops normal execution and unwinds the stack. Recover catches a panic inside a deferred function. Only use panics for truly exceptional, unrecoverable situations.

Goroutines: Lightweight concurrent execution managed by the Go runtime (not OS threads). Launch with go keyword. Goroutines share the same address space; use channels or sync primitives for coordination.
Channels: Typed conduits for goroutine communication. Use ch := make(chan T) to create. Send: ch <- v. Receive: v := <-ch. Block until both ends are ready.

ch := make(chan int)
go func() { ch <- 42 }()
value := <-ch // blocks until value sent
fmt.Println(value) // 42
Buffered Channels: Channels with capacity: make(chan T, cap). Send blocks only when buffer is full; receive blocks only when buffer is empty. Reduces synchronization points.

ch := make(chan int, 2)
ch <- 1
ch <- 2
// Non-blocking sends until buffer full
fmt.Println(<-ch) // 1
fmt.Println(<-ch) // 2
Range & Close: Sender closes a channel with close(ch). Receiver can range over the channel, receiving values until the channel is closed. Detect closed channels with v, ok := <-ch.
Select Statement: Wait on multiple channel operations simultaneously. Select blocks until one case is ready. Use default for non-blocking operations. Use nil channels to disable cases.

select {
case msg := <-ch1:
	fmt.Println(msg)
case msg := <-ch2:
	fmt.Println(msg)
case <-time.After(1 * time.Second):
	fmt.Println("timeout")
default:
	fmt.Println("no message ready")
}
WaitGroup: sync.WaitGroup blocks until all goroutines finish. Add(n) increments the counter, Done() decrements, Wait() blocks until counter reaches 0. Typically Add is called before starting goroutines.
sync.Once: sync.Once ensures a function is executed exactly once, even across multiple goroutines. Used for lazy initialization, singleton setup, and one-time configuration.
Mutex & RWMutex: sync.Mutex provides mutual exclusion. Lock/Unlock protects critical sections. sync.RWMutex allows multiple readers or one writer. RLock/RUnlock for read-only access.
Worker Pools: Fixed number of goroutines processing jobs from a channel. Controls concurrency, limits resource usage. Use a buffered channel for jobs and close it to signal completion.
Fan-in / Fan-out: Fan-out: multiple goroutines read from one channel (distributes work). Fan-in: multiple goroutines write to one channel (multiplexing results). Use a merge function with sync.WaitGroup.

Package Declaration: Every Go file belongs to a package. Executables use 'package main', libraries use any descriptive name. One directory = one package.
Importing Packages: Use import for dependencies. Standard library packages have short paths; remote packages use full module paths. go mod tidy manages required versions. Key tooling commands: go doc shows documentation for any package/symbol (go doc fmt.Println), go clean removes built artifacts (go clean -cache), go version prints the Go version. Use go doc for quick reference without leaving the terminal.
Exported Names: Capitalized names are exported (public), lowercase are unexported (package-private). Exported names are accessible across packages; unexported only within the same package.

type User struct{}      // Exported
type user struct{}      // Unexported
func Public() {}          // Exported
func private() {}         // Unexported
const MaxValue = 100      // Exported
const minValue = 1        // Unexported
Package Initialization (init): init() runs when a package is imported. Multiple init()s across a package run in file name order. init() functions cannot be called directly. They run before main().
Internal Packages: Packages under an 'internal/' directory are only importable by code rooted at the internal's parent. Enforces encapsulation boundaries within a module.

project/
└── internal/
    └── auth/
        └── token.go  // only importable by project/...

package internal/auth
// This can ONLY be imported by code inside project/
Blank Imports: Import a package solely for its side effects (init() execution) using _. The dot alias '.' imports all exported names into the current namespace.
Import Cycles: Go does not allow import cycles. A cannot import B if B imports A (directly or indirectly). Break cycles by extracting shared types into a third package, or using interfaces.

Reading Files (os.ReadFile): os.ReadFile (Go 1.16+) reads a file into memory. Replaces deprecated ioutil.ReadFile. Use for small files. For large files, use bufio.Scanner or io.Copy with limited buffer.
Writing Files (os.WriteFile): os.WriteFile writes data to a file, creating or truncating it. The third argument is file permissions (Unix mode). Replaces deprecated ioutil.WriteFile.
Buffered I/O (bufio): bufio provides buffered reading and writing for efficiency. bufio.Scanner reads line-by-line (default) or via SplitFunc. bufio.Writer buffers writes to reduce syscalls.
io.ReadAll: io.ReadAll reads from an io.Reader until EOF, returning the full byte slice. Replaces ioutil.ReadAll. Works with any reader: files, HTTP bodies, strings, etc.
io.Copy: io.Copy copies from an io.Reader to an io.Writer until EOF. Efficiently streams data without loading everything into memory. Returns bytes copied and any error.

src, _ := os.Open("source.txt")
defer src.Close()
dst, _ := os.Create("dest.txt")
defer dst.Close()

written, err := io.Copy(dst, src)
fmt.Printf("copied %d bytes\n", written)
File Permissions & ioutil Deprecation: ioutil is deprecated since Go 1.16. Replace ioutil.ReadFile with os.ReadFile, ioutil.WriteFile with os.WriteFile, ioutil.ReadAll with io.ReadAll, ioutil.TempFile with os.CreateTemp.
Directory Operations: Read directories with os.ReadDir (returns sorted []os.DirEntry). Walk directory trees with filepath.Walk or filepath.WalkDir. Create dirs with os.MkdirAll.

Test Functions: Write tests in *_test.go files. Test functions follow func TestXxx(t *testing.T). Use t.Error/t.Fatal for failures. Run with go test.
Table-Driven Tests: Define test cases as a slice of structs. Iterate over them for clean, DRY tests that cover many inputs. Each case can include a name for clear failure output.
Subtests: Run subtests with t.Run(name, fn) for hierarchical test organization. Subtests share setup/teardown and can be run selectively with go test -run pattern.
Test Helpers: Helper functions in tests reduce boilerplate. Call t.Helper() to mark a function as a test helper so failure line numbers point to the caller, not the helper.
Test Coverage: Go has built-in coverage. Run go test -cover to see percentage. go test -coverprofile=coverage.out generates a profile. Use go tool cover -html=coverage.out for visual report.

# Run with coverage
$ go test -cover ./...
# Output: ok  myapp/mypkg  0.002s  coverage: 85.2% of statements

# Generate HTML report
go test -coverprofile=coverage.out ./...
go tool cover -html=coverage.out -o coverage.html
Fuzzing: Go 1.18+ fuzzing randomly generates inputs to find bugs. Fuzz test: func FuzzXxx(f *testing.F). Seed with f.Add(), then f.Fuzz(targetFn).
Benchmarks: Measure performance with BenchmarkXxx(b *testing.B). b.N is adjusted by the framework for stable timing. Use b.ResetTimer() and b.ReportAllocs() for accurate measurements.

fmt Package: Formatted I/O with Print, Printf, Println, Sprintf, Fprintf. Verbs: %v (value), %+v (with fields), %T (type), %d (int), %s (string), %#v (Go-syntax).

fmt.Println("Hello")
fmt.Printf("Value: %d, Type: %T\n", 42, 42)
s := fmt.Sprintf("hex: %x", 255) // "ff"
fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "error: %v\n", err)
strings & strconv Packages: strings: Contains, Split, Join, ToUpper, ToLower, Trim, Replace, Builder (efficient string building). strconv: Atoi, Itoa, ParseBool, FormatFloat, ParseInt.

s := "hello world"
fmt.Println(strings.ToUpper(s))
parts := strings.Split(s, " ")

n, _ := strconv.Atoi("42")
s2 := strconv.Itoa(42)

var b strings.Builder
for i := 0; i < 100; i++ {
	b.WriteString("a")
}
fmt.Println(b.String())
io Package: Core I/O interfaces: io.Reader, io.Writer, io.Closer, io.Seeker. Utility functions: io.Copy, io.ReadAll, io.MultiReader, io.TeeReader, io.LimitReader.

var w io.Writer = os.Stdout
fmt.Fprint(w, "output")

// MultiReader chains readers
r := io.MultiReader(strings.NewReader("a"), strings.NewReader("b"))

// TeeReader mirrors reads to a writer
pr, pw := io.Pipe()
io.Copy(os.Stdout, pr) // reads from pr
encoding/json Package: Marshal/Unmarshal Go values to/from JSON. Struct tags control field names, omitempty skips zero values. Use json.NewDecoder for streaming JSON (files, HTTP).
flag Package: Parse command-line flags with flag package. Supports -flag, -flag=x, --flag (double dash works). Types: String, Int, Bool, Duration, Float64, or custom flag.Value.
log Package: Simple logging to stderr with timestamps. log.Printf, log.Fatalf (calls os.Exit(1)), log.Panicf (calls panic). Use log.New for custom output, flags, and prefix.
os/exec Package: Run external commands. exec.Command(name, args...). cmd.Output() returns stdout, cmd.CombinedOutput() returns both. Pipe stdin/stdout/stderr for interactive commands.

cmd := exec.Command("ls", "-la")
out, err := cmd.Output()
if err != nil {
	log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(string(out))

// With pipes
cmd.Stdin = strings.NewReader("input data")
cmd.Stdout = os.Stdout
cmd.Stderr = os.Stderr
cmd.Run()
time Package: Time and duration with nanosecond precision. Parse (reference time: Mon Jan 2 15:04:05 MST 2006 = 1 2 3 4 5 6 -7). Timer/Ticker for events. Sleep for pauses.
context Package: Context propagates deadlines, cancellation signals, and request-scoped values. Create with context.Background() or context.TODO(). Derive with WithCancel, WithTimeout, WithDeadline, WithValue.
sync Package: Synchronization primitives: Mutex, RWMutex, WaitGroup, Once, Cond, Pool, Map (concurrent-safe map). sync.Map is optimized for read-heavy or append-only patterns.

var mu sync.Mutex
var counter int

var wg sync.WaitGroup
for i := 0; i < 10; i++ {
	wg.Add(1)
	go func() {
		defer wg.Done()
		mu.Lock()
		counter++
		mu.Unlock()
	}()
}
wg.Wait()
fmt.Println("Counter:", counter)

Go Modules: Go modules define a project's dependencies and versioning. go.mod declares the module path and requirements. go.sum contains checksums for reproducibility. Cross-compilation is built-in: set GOOS and GOARCH env vars to target different platforms (GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build). Common targets: linux/amd64, darwin/amd64, darwin/arm64, windows/amd64. Use go tool dist list to see all supported targets. Cross-compilation doesn't require additional toolchains — Go includes all targets in the standard distribution.
Workspace Mode: Go 1.18+ workspace mode (go.work) lets you work on multiple modules simultaneously. Useful for local development across interdependent modules. go work init creates the file.

go.work file:
go 1.22

use (
	./myapp
	./sharedlib
	./tools
)

# Commands
$ go work init ./myapp ./sharedlib
$ go work use ./newmod
$ go work sync
Build Tags: Build tags (or build constraints) conditionally compile files. Placed at top of file: //go:build tag. Multiple tags combine with &&, ||, and !. Use for platform-specific code or feature flags.
go generate: go generate scans //go:generate directives to run tools automatically. Commonly used for code generation: protobufs, stringers, mocks, and embed. Run with go generate ./....
go tooling (vet, fmt, fix): go vet detects suspicious constructs (e.g., unreachable code, wrong Printf verbs). go fmt automatically formats code to canonical style. go fix updates old API usage to newer versions.

go vet ./...      # static analysis
# Detects: unreachable code, wrong Printf args, etc.

go fmt ./...      # formats all files
# Equivalent to: gofmt -l -w .

go fix ./...      # migrate deprecated APIs
go tool pprof     # CPU/memory profiling
go tool trace     # execution trace
Dependency Management (go get): go get manages module dependencies. Latest compatible version: go get pkg@latest. Specific version: go get pkg@v1.2.3. Upgrade minor: go get -u ./.... Remove unused: go mod tidy.

go get github.com/gorilla/mux@latest
# upgrades to latest tagged version

go get github.com/gorilla/mux@v1.8.0
# specific version

go get -u ./...
# upgrade all direct/indirect deps

go mod tidy
# removes unused deps, adds missing
Generics: Go 1.18+ supports type parameters for functions and types. Use constraints (interface with type sets) to restrict acceptable types. 'any' is a shortcut for interface{}. Comparable constraint for ==.

HTTP Server (net/http): Build HTTP servers with http.HandleFunc or http.Handler interface. http.ListenAndServe starts the server. Default mux is http.DefaultServeMux.
HTTP Client: http.Client with Get, Post, Do methods. Respect context cancellation, always close response body, set timeouts to avoid hanging connections.
Routing & ServeMux (Go 1.22+): Go 1.22 enhanced the default mux with method-based routing and path parameters using {param} and {param...} patterns.
Middleware Pattern: Middleware wraps http.Handler to add cross-cutting concerns: logging, auth, recovery, rate limiting, CORS. Use a function that takes and returns http.Handler.
Templates (html/template): html/template generates safe HTML output with automatic context-aware escaping. Use template.ParseFiles or template.New(). Execute with a data struct and func map.
TLS & HTTPS: Use http.ListenAndServeTLS to serve HTTPS. Generate self-signed certs with crypto/tls or use Let's Encrypt via autocert. Always serve HTTPS in production.
TCP & UDP Sockets: Low-level networking with net.Dial (TCP/UDP) and net.Listen. Build custom protocols. Use bufio for line-based protocols. Always set deadlines.

database/sql Interface: database/sql provides a generic SQL interface. Open a database with sql.Open (driver name + DSN). Use sql.DB for connection pooling. Run queries with Query, QueryRow, Exec.
Querying (Query & QueryRow): Query returns *sql.Rows (cursor). Iterate with rows.Next() and rows.Scan(). QueryRow returns at most one row, returns sql.ErrNoRows if none. Always close rows.
Prepared Statements: Prepare statements with db.Prepare for repeated execution. Prevents SQL injection and improves performance. Use $1, $2 (PostgreSQL) or ? (MySQL/SQLite) placeholders.
Transactions: Use db.Begin() to start a transaction. tx.Exec, tx.Query within the transaction. Commit or Rollback. Ensures atomicity — all operations succeed or none do.
Connection Pooling: sql.DB manages a connection pool. Configure with SetMaxOpenConns (max concurrent), SetMaxIdleConns (idle pool), SetConnMaxLifetime (connection age), SetConnMaxIdleTime.

db, _ := sql.Open("postgres", dsn)

// Tune the pool
db.SetMaxOpenConns(25)   // max simultaneous connections
db.SetMaxIdleConns(5)    // keep 5 idle
db.SetConnMaxLifetime(5 * time.Minute)  // recycle connections
db.SetConnMaxIdleTime(1 * time.Minute)   // close idle connections

// Ping checks a connection from the pool
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Second)
defer cancel()
db.PingContext(ctx)
Migrations (golang-migrate): Manage schema changes with migration tools like golang-migrate/migrate. Migration files: 001_create_users.up.sql and 001_create_users.down.sql. Run up/down programmatically via CLI.
Database Drivers: Register database drivers via blank imports. Common drivers: lib/pq (PostgreSQL), go-sql-driver/mysql (MySQL), mattn/go-sqlite3 (SQLite), mongo-driver (MongoDB).

Go Design Philosophy: Learning Go emphasizes simplicity: no inheritance, no generics (until 1.18), no exceptions. Go favors composition over inheritance, explicit error handling, and readability over cleverness. Bodner calls this 'the boring language that gets things done'. The key insight: Go is designed for large teams maintaining code over years.
nil & Zero Values Mental Model: Know Go teaches the nil mental model: nil is a value, not an error. Nil slices have len=0 and can append to. Nil maps return zero values but panic on write. Nil interfaces have dynamic type nil (not just value nil). A nil pointer inside an interface makes it non-nil! Book insight: always think about what zero value means for your types.
slog Structured Logging (Go 1.21+): slog provides structured, leveled logging with key-value pairs. Levels: Debug, Info, Warn, Error. Use slog.New with JSONHandler or TextHandler. slog.Group for nested keys. slog.Attr for reusable attributes. The book recommendation: always use structured logging for production.
errors.Join & Error Handling (Go 1.20+): errors.Join combines multiple errors into one. Useful for batch validation and deferred cleanup. Know Go emphasizes thinking of errors as values that can be combined. Also new: fmt.Errorf with multiple %w (Go 1.20+ can wrap multiple errors).
maps & slices Packages (Go 1.21+): Standard library packages for generic operations on maps and slices. No more hand-rolling Contains, DeleteFunc, Filter, etc. These are type-safe and efficient.
Range over Iterators & func (Go 1.23+): Go 1.23 adds range-over-iterator support. Any function with func(yield func(K, V) bool) can be ranged. The iter package provides Seq and Seq2 types. Libraries can expose iterators instead of requiring callbacks.
Embedding (//go:embed): go:embed embeds files into the binary at compile time. Supports files, directories, and globs. Embed as []byte, string, or embed.FS. Know Go recommends embed for static assets over reading files at runtime.
Race Detector & Data Races: The Go race detector catches concurrent unsafe access. Run with -race flag. Learning Go: if two goroutines access the same variable without synchronization, it's a race. Know Go says 'always run tests with -race before shipping'. The detector has ~false negative rate but no false positives.
Profiling & pprof: Go's built-in profiler: CPU, memory, goroutine, mutex, block profiles. Learning Go: always profile before optimizing. Use net/http/pprof for web apps, runtime/pprof for CLIs. The book's advice: 'measure, don't guess'.
sync/atomic (Go 1.19+ Typed API): Go 1.19+ added typed atomic values: atomic.Int64, atomic.Value, etc. Learning Go recommends them over sync.Mutex for simple counters and flags. The zero value is ready to use, no initialization needed.

CLI Applications (Cobra): Build powerful CLI applications with Cobra (spf13/cobra), the framework behind kubectl, gh, and hugo. Cobra handles commands, flags, subcommands, and help generation. Commands are structured as a tree with Run functions. Use PersistentFlags for flags shared across subcommands and LocalFlags for command-specific ones. Best practice: organize commands in a cmd/ directory; use Viper (spf13/viper) with Cobra for config file support.
Web Frameworks (Gin, Echo): While net/http suffices for many cases, frameworks like Gin (gin-gonic/gin) and Echo (labstack/echo) add routing with parameters, middleware chaining, request binding/validation, and grouped routes. Gin uses a radix tree router for high performance. Echo has built-in middleware for CORS, logging, recovery, and CSRF. Common mistake: adding a framework when the standard library would suffice — start with net/http and add a framework only when you need advanced routing or middleware. Best practice: use Gin for REST APIs with JSON; use Echo if you prefer a more minimalist API.
gRPC & Protocol Buffers: gRPC is a high-performance RPC framework using HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers for serialization. Define services in .proto files, generate Go code with protoc. Supports four service types: unary, server-streaming, client-streaming, and bidirectional streaming. Common mistake: using gRPC for browser clients without gRPC-Web — browsers don't support HTTP/2 trailers directly. Best practice: use gRPC for internal microservices communication; use REST/JSON for external/public APIs; always set deadlines on gRPC calls to prevent hanging.
Logging Libraries (Zap, Zerolog): For high-performance structured logging, Zap (uber-go/zap) and Zerolog (rs/zerolog) offer zero-allocation logging paths. Zap claims to be 10x faster than the standard log package in its SugaredLogger mode and 100x faster in its Logger mode. Zerolog uses a chained API. Both support leveled logging (Debug, Info, Warn, Error), structured fields, and JSON output. Best practice: use slog (standard library, Go 1.21+) for most applications; reach for Zap or Zerolog when profiling shows logging is a bottleneck.
Linters & Code Quality: Maintain code quality with automated tools. golangci-lint runs multiple linters in parallel (staticcheck, revive, govet, errcheck, ineffassign, and 30+ more). staticcheck is a curated set of advanced vet checks. govulncheck scans dependencies for known CVEs. Best practice: run golangci-lint in CI for every PR; use golangci-lint run --fix to auto-fix issues; run govulncheck ./... before deploying to catch vulnerable dependencies.

Reflection: The reflect package allows inspecting and manipulating types and values at runtime. Use reflect.TypeOf to get type information, reflect.ValueOf to get the value. Common use cases: serialization (encoding/json uses reflection), testing frameworks, and generic utilities. Common mistake: overusing reflection — it's slow, breaks type safety, and makes code hard to understand. Best practice: avoid reflection unless absolutely necessary; prefer type assertions, interfaces, or code generation (go generate) over reflect.

import "reflect"

var x float64 = 3.14
t := reflect.TypeOf(x)
v := reflect.ValueOf(x)

fmt.Println(t)        // float64
fmt.Println(v.Float()) // 3.14

// Inspect struct tags
type Config struct {
	Port int `json:"port" default:"8080"`
}

field, _ := reflect.TypeOf(Config{}).FieldByName("Port")
fmt.Println(field.Tag.Get("json"))    // "port"
fmt.Println(field.Tag.Get("default")) // "8080"
CGO Basics: CGO lets Go call C code directly. Use import "C" with special comments (// #include ...) above it. CGO requires a C compiler and adds build complexity. Common use cases: linking with native libraries (SDL, OpenSSL), performance-critical sections, and system calls not exposed by Go. Common mistake: using CGO when a pure Go alternative exists — prefer cgo-free builds (CGO_ENABLED=0) for simpler cross-compilation. Best practice: isolate CGO code behind a pure Go interface; use //go:build cgo build tags for conditional compilation.
Escape Analysis: Escape analysis is the compiler's optimization that determines whether a value can be allocated on the stack (fast, no GC overhead) or must be on the heap (GC-managed). A value escapes if its pointer is returned, stored in a global, or passed to a function that stores it. Use go build -gcflags='-m' to see escape analysis decisions. Common mistake: assuming small values stay on the stack — if a pointer escapes, even an int goes to the heap. Best practice: prefer value receivers over pointer receivers for small structs; avoid returning pointers to local variables when possible; use -gcflags='-m' to check your assumptions.
unsafe Package: The unsafe package provides low-level primitives for bypassing Go's type safety. unsafe.Pointer converts between arbitrary pointer types. uintptr is an integer type for pointer arithmetic. Common use cases: efficient serialization, interacting with C libraries via CGO, and performance-critical hot paths. Common mistake: using unsafe for ordinary code — it breaks the memory safety guarantees that make Go reliable. Best practice: avoid unsafe in application code; if you must use it, keep it confined to a small, well-tested package with a safe public API; never use uintptr after the referenced object is garbage collected.

import "unsafe"

// Size and offset of struct fields
type Data struct {
	X int64 // 8 bytes
	Y bool  // 1 byte (+7 padding)
}

fmt.Println(unsafe.Sizeof(Data{}))     // 16 (with alignment)
fmt.Println(unsafe.Offsetof(Data{}.Y)) // 8

// Pointer arithmetic (careful!)
var arr [3]int32
base := unsafe.Pointer(&arr[0])
second := (*int32)(unsafe.Pointer(uintptr(base) + unsafe.Sizeof(arr[0])))
*second = 42
fmt.Println(arr[1]) // 42

// Converting between types
var f float64 = 3.14
bits := *(*uint64)(unsafe.Pointer(&f))
fmt.Printf("%016x\n", bits) // float64 bits as uint64

Docker Multi-stage Builds: Use multi-stage Docker builds to create minimal Go images. Stage 1: build the binary with golang:alpine. Stage 2: copy the binary to scratch or distroless (no OS, ~5MB image). Key benefits: tiny attack surface, fast deployment, no build tools in production. Common mistake: using ubuntu or full golang images in production — adds 300MB+ of unnecessary weight. Best practice: use scratch for pure Go binaries; use gcr.io/distroless/base if you need libc (CGO); use alpine:3.x if you need a shell and common tools; always set CGO_ENABLED=0 for static linking.

# Dockerfile
FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build -o /app/server .

FROM scratch
COPY --from=builder /app/server /server
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["/server"]

# Build
# $ docker build -t myapp .
# $ docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp

# With distroless
# FROM gcr.io/distroless/base-debian12
# COPY --from=builder /app/server /server
Kubernetes Deployment: Deploy Go services to Kubernetes with Deployments (replicas, rolling updates) and Services (networking). Use liveness probes to restart unhealthy pods and readiness probes to route traffic only when ready. ConfigMaps and Secrets inject configuration. Common practice: expose metrics via Prometheus on a separate port, use healthz/readyz endpoints for probes, and set resource limits. Best practice: use client-go for in-cluster Go clients; always set context.WithTimeout for database and HTTP calls within pods; use the --restart=Never flag for one-shot jobs.

# deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: go-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: go-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: go-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: myapp:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 8080 }
        resources:
          limits: { cpu: 500m, memory: 256Mi }
          requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: go-api
spec:
  selector:
    app: go-api
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080

# Deploy
# $ kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
# $ kubectl get pods
# $ kubectl rollout status deployment/go-api
